_why: The inherited genres came from a Wikipedia-derived dataset that mixed a book's primary genre with whatever else had ever been said about it. The Fellowship of the Ring was filed under 'Autobiography; Biography; Reference'. The Invisible Man under 'Albino bias'. Dracula, Beloved, The Shining, The Stand, Brave New World and The Old Man and the Sea were all 'Children's literature'. The 48 Laws of Power had no genres at all, and East of Eden had only 'Novel'. These 60 are re-tagged by hand.
_rules: Two to three labels per book: what it IS, then what it is ABOUT.
Every label must carry at least 2 books. A label with one carrier is a dead end -- a reader who read that book gets no neighbour from it.
No label may carry more than 20 of the 60. Past a third of the shelf a subject stops distinguishing, which is the rule taste_profile already applies.
No 'Fiction', 'Novel' or 'Literary' -- normalize_subjects discards them, and rightly: they describe every book here.

Avoid any label ending in ' fiction'. normalize_subjects strips that suffix, so 'Science fiction' would collapse into 'science' and collide with the topic, and 'Literary fiction' would become 'literary' and be dropped entirely.

A label must mean the same thing in every book that carries it. A Game of Thrones was first tagged 'Power' for its politics, which put The 48 Laws of Power in front of a reader who had just finished The Hobbit -- the word matched, the meaning did not.

Tag the book as it is read now, not as it was published. The Hobbit is a children's book by history, and tagging it so offered Charlotte's Web and Diary of a Wimpy Kid to a reader who had just finished A Game of Thrones.
